summaries.example: Imagine a wooden board. It could become a table or a bowl. Aristotle would say the wood has the potential to become different things. When a craftsperson gives it the right shape, one possibility becomes actual. The wood is the material, and the shape helps make it the kind of thing it is.
summaries.summary: Aristotle’s Metaphysics asks big questions about what exists and what makes things what they are. Aristotle calls this project “first philosophy.” It studies beings in a very general way, not just as changing objects or measurable objects. He gives special importance to substances, such as individual animals, plants, and other independent things. Qualities, sizes, and relationships depend on substances. To explain change and identity, Aristotle describes things as combinations of matter and form. Matter is what something is made from; form is the organization or character that makes it the kind of thing it is. He also distinguishes potentiality from actuality. A seed may potentially become a plant, while a grown plant is an actual living thing. Aristotle examines causes, definitions, unity, universals, and the principle that something cannot both have and lack the same feature in the same respect at the same time. He also discusses theology as the study of an eternal, unchanging substance, though the connection between theology and the general study of being is difficult and has been debated by scholars.
key_ideas: Aristotle’s first philosophy asks about the deepest causes and starting points of reality.
He says “being” has several related meanings, with substance as the most important kind.
Things are often understood through matter and form: what they are made of and how they are organized.
A thing can be potentially something before it becomes that thing actually.
Aristotle connects the study of reality with very basic rules of thinking, including that the same thing cannot both be and not be in the same way at the same time.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aristotle’s questions help us notice that an object is not explained only by its material pieces. We can also ask what structure, purpose, activity, or possibility makes it the thing it is. These ideas influenced later thinking about science, change, explanation, definitions, and reality. The entry also shows that important philosophical books may contain hard questions without giving one simple answer to every problem.

important_terms.definition: The study of what it means for things to be, considered in a very general way.
A basic, independent thing, such as an animal or a plant, according to Aristotle’s framework.
The material and organization that make something the kind of thing it is.
The stuff from which something is made, such as wood in a table.
A possibility or capacity to become or do something.
Being fully realized or active rather than merely possible.

questions_to_think_about: Can one object be made from different materials and still be the same kind of thing?
Is a thing more than the pieces that make it up?
What is the difference between being able to do something and actually doing it?
Why might philosophers want to study the most general features of everything that exists?

summaries.example: Consider a house made from bricks and timber. Its matter is the material that composes it, but the house is not identical with a mere pile of those materials. Its form is the organized structure and plan that make the materials a house. The form can also explain why the materials constitute a house and, in the case of an artifact, can be present in the builder’s craft or design. Aristotle’s analysis therefore treats the form as central to the house’s being, while still recognizing the role of matter in its production.
summaries.summary: Aristotle’s Metaphysics presents first philosophy as the inquiry into beings insofar as they are beings. It seeks the most fundamental causes and principles, rather than focusing on one restricted domain such as motion or quantity. A central difficulty is that “being” is said in many ways. Aristotle’s proposed solution is that these senses are not unrelated ambiguities; they are ordered around a primary sense, substance. In the Categories, substances are independent subjects, while qualities, quantities, and relations exist in or depend on them. The Metaphysics revisits this account and asks what substance itself is. Aristotle considers the subject, matter, form, essence, genus, and universal as candidates. His later analysis treats sensible substances as hylomorphic compounds of matter and form. Matter is what can receive organization; form is the essence or organizing principle that makes the compound the kind of thing it is. This framework explains generation, definition, causal explanation, and unity. It also supports Aristotle’s distinction between potentiality and actuality: capacities are intelligible in relation to their realized states, and actuality is prior in account and, in important respects, in substance. A major interpretive tension concerns universals. Form seems connected with definability and therefore universality, yet Aristotle argues that universals are not substances. Scholars disagree about how these claims fit together. The work also connects first philosophy with theology: if an eternal, separate, immovable substance exists, its activity can serve as a highest explanatory principle. Aristotle describes this primary divine activity as self-understanding, but the entry emphasizes that the larger argument and its interpretation are complex.
key_ideas: First philosophy studies beings generally, unlike natural science, which studies changing material things, or mathematics, which studies things under the aspect of being measurable.
Being is not a single genus with one uniform definition. Its meanings are related to a central case: substance.
Aristotle’s Categories presents substances as primary subjects on which qualities, quantities, and relations depend. The Metaphysics then asks what makes a substance a substance.
Individual material substances are analyzed as hylomorphic compounds: matter together with form. Form is tied to essence, definition, and the explanation of a thing’s being.
Aristotle argues that actuality is prior to potentiality in account, and also in a deeper sense of being. A potentiality is understood through the actuality toward which it is directed.

The text develops a theology of an eternal, immovable substance whose essence is activity and whose thought is directed toward what is most excellent, while the relation between this theology and universal metaphysics remains interpretively difficult.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aristotle offers a model of philosophy that asks not only whether something exists, but what kind of being it has, what it depends on, and what explains its unity and activity. His distinctions between substance and attribute, matter and form, and potentiality and actuality became enduring tools for discussing identity, change, causation, definition, and scientific explanation. The entry also illustrates how a philosophical system can contain productive tensions—especially about universals and theology—rather than functioning as a set of completely settled doctrines.

important_terms.definition: Aristotle’s inquiry into beings insofar as they are beings, including their causes and principles; he also calls it first philosophy.
A primary, independent entity; in Aristotle’s framework, other categories depend on substances.
The “what it is to be” a thing: its intrinsic character, closely connected with definition.
The material component of a compound, understood as what is capable of receiving a form.
The organizing principle or essence that makes a thing the kind of thing it is.
A capacity or possibility, including a capacity to become a more complete state.
The realized state or exercise of a capacity; Aristotle gives it priority over potentiality in several respects.
A basic rule of reasoning stating that the same thing cannot both belong and not belong to the same subject, in the same respect, at the same time.

questions_to_think_about: If being has several meanings, what makes a single science of being possible?
Can a substantial form be universal if Aristotle also says that no universal is a substance?
Does matter alone explain what an object is, or does form provide the more important explanation?
Why does Aristotle think a definition must express an essence rather than merely explain a word?
How does the priority of actuality shape Aristotle’s account of natural development and change?

summaries.example: Suppose a student builds a model bridge from craft sticks. The sticks are its matter, but a random pile of sticks is not yet a bridge. The design and arrangement give the pieces a form that lets the whole serve as a bridge. Before building, the sticks are potentially part of a bridge. After the design is realized, the bridge exists actually. Aristotle would ask whether the bridge’s materials, design, purpose, or builder best explains what it is; his account allows several kinds of causes to work together.
summaries.summary: Aristotle’s Metaphysics investigates the most general features of reality. Aristotle describes this inquiry as first philosophy, the study of being qua being, wisdom, and—in one important sense—theology. “Being qua being” means studying things simply as beings, rather than studying them only as moving, changing, or measurable. Aristotle argues that being has several connected meanings. Substance is central because it is the primary kind of being: qualities, amounts, and relations belong to substances or depend on them. The work then asks what makes something a substance. Aristotle considers a subject, matter, form, essence, genus, and universal. His later account treats ordinary things as combinations of matter and form. Matter is what can take on organization; form is what makes the thing the kind of thing it is and is closely linked with essence and definition. This helps explain how things come to be. A builder does not create the wood or bricks from nothing, and does not create the plan in the same way; the builder organizes matter according to a form, producing a complete object. Aristotle also explains causes in several ways: what something is made of, what structure it has, what brings it about, and what it is for. Potentiality and actuality describe what a thing can become and what it has realized. Aristotle gives actuality priority in several arguments. Finally, he discusses whether universals can be substances and connects first philosophy with a separate, eternal, unmoving substance. The entry presents these claims as parts of a difficult work whose interpretations remain disputed.
key_ideas: Aristotle calls metaphysics “first philosophy” because it studies fundamental causes and principles, not because it is necessarily the first subject students study.
He compares different sciences by asking what aspect of beings each studies: nature studies change, mathematics studies measurable features, and metaphysics studies beings generally.
Substance has a privileged role because other features, such as colors or sizes, depend on substances rather than existing independently.
Aristotle’s account develops from simple subjects in the Categories to matter-form compounds in the Metaphysics.
He gives several meanings to “cause,” including material, formal, moving, and final causes. One thing can have more than one kind of cause.
Aristotle’s discussion of universals, definitions, and divine activity contains questions that interpreters continue to debate.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aristotle’s framework gives readers several ways to explain one thing instead of assuming that every explanation must have only one cause. It also encourages careful questions about dependence: does a property exist on its own, or only in something else? His distinctions remain useful for thinking about change, design, identity, possibility, and the difference between an object and the materials that compose it. Just as importantly, the entry models how philosophers examine arguments whose parts may not fit together easily.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of what exists and what it means for something to be a being.
An independent thing that serves as a subject for properties, such as a particular animal or plant.
What something is made from; in Aristotle’s later account, matter can receive different forms.
The organization or defining character that makes something the kind of thing it is.
The basic nature of a thing, or what it is in itself rather than by accident.
A capacity to become or do something, even if that capacity is not currently realized.
A realized condition or activity, as opposed to something that is merely possible.
A fundamental principle used in reasoning; Aristotle especially discusses the rule against contradiction.

questions_to_think_about: How is a quality, such as a color, different from the object that has that color?
Could a general idea, such as “animal,” be a real substance, or is it dependent on individual animals?
Which explains a bridge better: its materials, its design, its builder, or its purpose?
Why might Aristotle say that a possibility is understood through the completed thing it could become?
What problems arise when Aristotle treats form as both a universal and the substance of a thing?
